output:
**What I found**
Don't cut the pool (the record calls this Reject). The 22% that looks idle is the headroom that keeps queue waits at their current level. Your jobs currently keep 7.8 runners busy on average (10 × 0.78). With 8 runners the same work puts average utilization at 97.5%. Queue wait grows roughly as ρ/(1−ρ). That factor goes from 3.5 at 78% to 39 at 97.5%, so expect average waits around 11× worse, not slightly worse.

The afternoon is worse still. Fitting the same curve to your two waits (9 min overall, 31 min from 14:00 to 17:00) puts afternoon utilization near 92%, which is about 9.2 runners of demand. An 8-runner pool can't keep up with that. The backlog would grow for the whole three hours, about 1.2 runners × 180 min ≈ 216 runner-minutes. That adds roughly 27 more minutes of wait by 17:00, on top of today's 31, and it spills into the evening. This is an estimate from the curve, not a simulation. The real numbers will probably be worse because merges arrive in bursts.

**Why it matters**
Cutting saves the cost of 2 runners. In exchange, waits roughly double in the afternoon, when most merges land. Developers waiting on merges cost far more than two runners, and longer waits push people to batch their merges, which makes the bursts worse. Leaving things as they are also has a cost: the afternoon queue (31 min) already takes longer than the job itself (12 min). The pool is too small at peak and too big at night, so finance is right that some capacity is wasted, just in the wrong hours.

**Do this first**
1. Get runner utilization per hour from the CI metrics for the same 30 days. If the 78% is a 24-hour average, nights are mostly idle and the afternoon is even busier than estimated. That would point to scaling by time of day instead of a flat cut: fewer runners off-peak, at least 10 from 14:00 to 17:00. That gives finance the savings without the afternoon pile-up.
2. Follow-up: make each job cheaper so the demand at peak shrinks. Options are caching, skipping jobs whose inputs haven't changed, and not re-running the same work at the merge step. Every minute cut from the 12-minute job lowers peak utilization directly.

**What I did not check**
- Utilization by hour and whether the 78% covers 24 hours or working hours only. The hourly export from step 1 closes this.
- How bursty job arrivals are. The same export, bucketed into 5-minute windows, closes this.
- What a runner costs compared with what an hour of developer waiting costs. Ask finance for the runner cost per month, and estimate jobs per day × extra wait × loaded hourly rate.
- No queueing simulation was run. All figures come from the utilization curve and a simple backlog estimate.

```
Scope:          Shared CI runner pool (10 runners), last 30 days
Constraint:     Runner capacity during 14:00–17:00 (estimated ρ ≈ 0.92, wait 31 min > 12 min job time)
Decision:       Reject (cut to 8). Optimize capacity by time of day instead.
Flow signal:    Utilization 0.78 avg → 0.975 at 8 runners; wait factor 3.5 → 39 (~11×);
                peak demand ≈ 9.2 runners > 8 → backlog grows ~216 runner-min over 3 h;
                variation: predictable daily peak (merge timing), not a one-off event
Evidence:       User-supplied 30-day figures: 12 min job, 9 min avg wait, 31 min peak wait,
                steady jobs/day, workload unchanged
Next action:    Export hourly runner utilization; if nights are underused, scale down
                off-peak and keep ≥10 runners from 14:00–17:00
Verification:   Not run (no metrics access). Check the queue-wait percentiles for 14:00–17:00
                before and after any capacity change
Residual risk:  Peak estimate assumes the curve's scaling holds for a 10-runner pool;
                bursty arrivals would make the cut worse than estimated
```
